newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: EA-Generali set to buy Creditanstalt.
newsitem.headline: EA-Generali set to buy Creditanstalt.

text.p: News that one of two reported bidders for Austrian sell-off candidate Creditanstalt did not undertake a due diligence study indicate the bank will be sold to a group led by insurer EA-Generali, analysts said on Friday.

Finance Minister Viktor Klima said earlier that a group of bidders led by Austro-Italian insurer EA-Generali would finish its final examination of Creditanstalt's books on Monday, while a second bidder had decided not to participate in the due diligence process.
"I've always wondered whether he really received a second offer," said a London-based banking analyst, speaking on condition of anonymity. "Nobody's interested six years on. You kind of lose it."

Finance ministry assurances that the submission of a final offer for the state's 70 percent voting stake in the bank was not conditional upon participation in the due diligence process did little to convince market sources, most of whom believe the sale of the bank, first planned in 1991, is a done deal.
"With such a big investment it would be extraordinary to forego the due diligence," said an Austrian analyst.
Klima earlier this month said he had received two indicative bids for the bank in the latest tender which is to close on December 16.

The consortium led by EA-Generali, which includes Commerzbank of Germany, Banca Commerciale Italiana and Austrian savings bank Die Erste has offered between 720 and 730 schillings a share -- a total of about 10 billion schillings, for two thirds of the state's 19.9 million ordinary shares in Creditanstalt.

A study by JP Morgan, the government's advisor in the sale, has valued the state's entire stake at 18 billion schillings ($1.67 billion), including a premium of five billion schillings for majority control of the bank.

No details of the second alleged bidder have emerged. Local media over the past few weeks named GE Capital, a unit of GE Corp., Citibank, BankAmerica and Germany's Deutsche Bank as potential buyers, but none of these rumours was ever confirmed.
Analysts said Klima was likely to have used the threat of a rival bid to force EA-Generali and its partners to up their bid.

Klima in September rejected the group's previous bid, reported to have been a similar version of their current bid, because he wanted to sell the stake in its entirety. He has since indicated he may be more flexible this time around. ($1=10.79 Schilling)
